questions.stem: Which of the following is a metric on $\mathbb{R}^2$?

options.explanation: This satisfies all three metric axioms. The triangle inequality holds because $\max(|x_i - z_i|) \le \max(|x_i - y_i|) + \max(|y_i - z_i|)$.
This is the square of the Euclidean distance. It fails the triangle inequality: take $x=(0,0)$, $y=(1,0)$, $z=(2,0)$. Then $d(x,z)=4$, $d(x,y)+d(y,z)=1+1=2 < 4$.
This is not always non-negative: take $x=(0,0)$, $y=(1,2)$. Then $d(x,y) = 1 - 2 = -1 < 0$. Metrics must be non-negative.
A metric must be defined on all pairs of points in the space, including $x = y$, where any metric must give 0.

questions.stem: The sequence of functions $f_n(x) = x^n$ on $[0, 1]$ converges pointwise to $f(x) = 0$ for $x \in [0,1)$ and $f(1) = 1$. Is this convergence uniform?

options.text: No — the limit function is not continuous, so the convergence cannot be uniform.
options.explanation: Uniform convergence preserves continuity. Since each $f_n$ is continuous but the limit $f$ is discontinuous at $x=1$, the convergence cannot be uniform on $[0,1]$.

options.text: Yes — for any $\varepsilon > 0$, we can find $N$ such that $|x^n - f(x)| < \varepsilon$ for all $n > N$ and all $x$.
options.explanation: We cannot: for any fixed $n$, $x^n$ is close to 1 for $x$ near 1. For $\varepsilon = 1/2$: no single $N$ works, because $x^n \to 1$ as $x \to 1^-$ for fixed $n$.
The convergence IS uniform on $[0, r]$ for any fixed $r < 1$, but the question asks about $[0,1]$.

options.text: The question is ill-posed because the limit is not a function.
options.explanation: The limit is a well-defined function on $[0,1]$: $f(x) = 0$ for $x < 1$ and $f(1) = 1$. It is just not continuous.

questions.stem: The Heine-Borel theorem (in $\mathbb{R}^n$) states that a set is compact if and only if it is:

options.explanation: In $\mathbb{R}^n$, compactness is equivalent to being closed (contains all its limit points) and bounded (fits inside some ball). This fails in infinite-dimensional spaces.
Open sets are not compact in general: the open interval $(0,1)$ is bounded but not compact (the cover $(1/n, 1)$ has no finite subcover).
Connected and bounded does not imply compactness: $(0,1)$ is connected and bounded but not compact.
This is the characterisation of compactness in general metric spaces, but Heine-Borel specifically refers to the simpler characterisation in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

questions.stem: A bounded function $f: [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is Riemann integrable if and only if:

options.text: The infimum of upper sums equals the supremum of lower sums over all partitions.
options.explanation: This is Riemann's criterion. The common value, when it exists, is the integral. Equivalently: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a partition $P$ with $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$.
Continuity is sufficient but not necessary. Monotone functions and functions with finitely many discontinuities are also Riemann integrable.
Having an antiderivative is not equivalent to Riemann integrability. A function can have an antiderivative but fail to be Riemann integrable (though Lebesgue integrability is then guaranteed).

options.text: $f$ is bounded and has at most countably many discontinuities.
options.explanation: This is a sufficient condition (Lebesgue's criterion for Riemann integrability: $f$ is integrable iff its set of discontinuities has measure zero) but is a stronger statement than the definition.
